So do not fear; I will provide for you and your little ones.” Thus he comforted them and spoke kindly to them.
50.overview:
Genesis 50 is the final chapter of Genesis and the conclusion of the Joseph narrative—and it brings both to their respective climaxes. Jacob is buried in Canaan, carried there by the covenant family and an Egyptian honor guard, fulfilling his last request. The brothers, fearful after Jacob’s death, send a message pleading for forgiveness. Joseph’s response contains the single most important sentence of the entire Joseph narrative—and perhaps of the entire book of Genesis: “You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good” (v.20).

This sentence is the key to the entire narrative. It does not excuse the brothers’ sin (“you meant evil”). It does not minimize the suffering (“against me”). It locates both within a larger divine purpose (“but God meant it for good”). The doctrine of providence is not that God turns good intentions into good outcomes; it is that God turns evil intentions into outcomes he intended for good. The very malice of the brothers was the instrument of God’s saving purpose—and this pattern is the pattern of the cross.

The chapter closes with Joseph’s death and his own burial request: do not leave my bones in Egypt. Like his father, Joseph stakes his body on the promise of the land. “God will surely visit you, and you shall carry up my bones from here” (v.25). The Exodus will fulfill this request (Ex 13:19; Josh 24:32). Genesis closes with a coffin in Egypt—but it is a coffin that awaits resurrection, a promise that awaits fulfillment. The story is not over; it is between the promise and the fulfillment, exactly where God’s people always live.

verseByVerse.heading: Jacob's Burial in Canaan
verseByVerse.content: Jacob’s embalming (forty days) and the Egyptians’ mourning (seventy days) give him a burial of state—an Egyptian honor that reflects Joseph’s standing. The procession to Canaan is extraordinary: Pharaoh’s servants, the elders of his household, all the elders of Egypt, plus the covenant family. Only the livestock and the children remain in Goshen. The nations mourn with Israel for the patriarch. The mourning at Atad is so great that the Canaanites rename the place Abel Mizraim (“mourning of Egypt”). Jacob is buried in the cave of Machpelah, as he commanded. The covenant patriarch is placed in the covenant land. His bones wait there for the resurrection.

verseByVerse.heading: The Brothers' Fear
verseByVerse.content: The brothers’ fear after Jacob’s death is revealing: they have never been fully certain of Joseph’s forgiveness. They assume that Jacob’s presence restrained Joseph and that now his death removes the restraint. They send a message attributing to Jacob a command to forgive—a command Jacob apparently never explicitly gave in the narrative (though Jacob’s knowledge of the sale is debated). Whether the message is genuine or fabricated, the brothers finally make the direct petition they never made in the original reconciliation: “Please forgive the transgression of your brothers and their sin, because they did evil to you.” The explicit naming of the evil (“they did evil to you”) is itself progress: they do not euphemize it.

verseByVerse.heading: "God Meant It for Good"
verseByVerse.content: “Do not fear, for am I in the place of God?” (v.19). Joseph’s first response to the brothers’ fear is theological: he is not God; retributive justice is not his to administer. His second response is the interpretive key of the entire narrative: “You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring it about that many people should be kept alive, as they are today” (v.20). The three elements are precise: the brothers’ evil intent (real), the divine good intent (equally real), and the concrete outcome (many lives preserved). Then the pastoral response: “I will provide for you and your little ones.” The doctrine of providence is embodied in continued practical care. He comforts them and speaks kindly—the Hebrew al-leb, “to the heart.”

verseByVerse.heading: Joseph's Last Words and Death
verseByVerse.content: Joseph lives 110 years, sees Ephraim’s children to the third generation, and sees the children of Manasseh’s son Machir placed on his knees—the adoption gesture of blessing. He has seen the fruitfulness of the covenant family multiply in Egypt. His final words are both theological and prophetic: “God will surely visit you, and you shall carry up my bones from here” (v.25). The paqad yipqod—“God will surely visit”—is the same verb the angels use in the Exodus (Ex 3:16; 13:19). The Exodus generation carries out Joseph’s bones; Joshua buries them at Shechem (Josh 24:32). Genesis ends with a coffin in Egypt. But it is a coffin pointed toward Canaan.

verseByVerse.heading: The End That Is a Beginning
verseByVerse.content: Genesis closes with a coffin in a foreign land. This is the deliberately unresolved ending: the promise of the land, of offspring, of blessing to all nations—none of it fully accomplished. The covenant family is in Egypt, not Canaan. The nation has not yet been formed. The blessing to all nations has barely begun. The coffin in Egypt is not failure; it is the form that faith takes at the end of the first act. It is the seed in the ground awaiting spring. Exodus will begin with the fulfillment of Joseph’s word (“God will surely visit you”) and the carrying of Joseph’s bones toward the promised land. The story of Genesis is the story of promise; the rest of the Bible is its fulfillment.

50.theology:
“You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good” (v.20) is the hermeneutical key to the Joseph narrative and the paradigm for all Christian theology of suffering and providence. The sentence has two subjects with two intentions applied to the same events: human malice and divine purpose coexist in the same sequence of events without either annulling the other. This is the doctrine of concursive providence: God works through secondary causes, including sinful ones, without being the author of the sin or the sin being less than sin.

The New Testament applies this paradigm explicitly to the cross: “this Jesus, delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men” (Acts 2:23). The crucifixion was simultaneously the most evil act in human history (the murder of the Son of God) and the most purposeful act in divine history (the salvation of the world). Joseph’s “you meant evil; God meant good” is the pre-figuring grammar of this paradox. Calvary is the ultimate vindication of the doctrine Joseph articulates in Egypt.

Joseph’s bones in a coffin in Egypt are the final image of Genesis—faith in the form of an unanswered promise. Hebrews 11:22 names this as faith: “By faith Joseph, at the end of his life, made mention of the exodus of the Israelites and gave directions concerning his bones.” The bones are carried for 430 years before they reach their rest at Shechem. The patience of faith is measured in centuries. The God who is faithful across centuries is the God Genesis exists to reveal.
50.examples:
Joseph’s “am I in the place of God?” (v.19) is the check on every impulse toward personal retribution. He has the power to destroy his brothers; he recognizes that retributive justice is not his to administer. This is not weakness but theological clarity: vengeance belongs to God (Deut 32:35; Rom 12:19). The one who has been most wronged is often the most tempted to make himself the judge. Joseph refuses the role—not because the wrong was not real but because the role is not his. Christian forgiveness operates the same way: it does not pretend the wrong did not happen; it refuses to carry the burden of executing judgment that belongs to God.

The closing coffin of Genesis is a perpetual invitation to live by promise rather than by possession. The patriarchs possessed almost nothing of what was promised—a cave of Machpelah, a well at Beersheba, a field at Shechem. They saw the promises from afar and greeted them (Heb 11:13). This is the posture of the whole people of God between the first and second comings of Christ: we possess the firstfruits (Rom 8:23), but not yet the full harvest; we have the down payment (2 Cor 1:22), but not yet the inheritance. We live with Joseph’s bones in Egypt—carried forward by the promise of the God who will surely visit us.

51.title: About This Commentary
51.overview:
This commentary on Genesis was prepared as a devotional and theological companion for personal and group study. It follows the same approach as the Ephesians, Isaiah, Acts, Ecclesiastes, Matthew, John, and Proverbs commentaries in this series: Reformed, evangelical, and doxological — written to glorify God and to help readers encounter the living Christ in every chapter of Scripture.

The commentary draws on the following primary sources: Timothy Keller's Genesis sermon series (Redeemer Presbyterian Church, New York); John Calvin, Commentary on the First Book of Moses Called Genesis; Derek Kidner, Genesis (Tyndale Old Testament Commentaries); Bruce Waltke, Genesis: A Commentary; Gordon Wenham, Genesis (Word Biblical Commentary, 2 vols.); and Alistair Begg. The christological reading follows the New Testament's own interpretive lead: Romans 5 (Adam and Christ), Romans 4 and Galatians 3 (Abraham's faith), Hebrews 11 (the patriarchs), and Hebrews 7 (Melchizedek).
